paper_a.title: Accelerating Stochastic Gradient Descent using Predictive Variance Reduction

paper_b.title: A Stochastic Gradient Method with an Exponential Convergence Rate for Finite Training Sets

metadata.description: Two competing variance-reduction frameworks for the same finite-sum smooth strongly-convex optimization problem. Both achieve linear convergence at the cost of one full-data pass per amortized stage. SAG (paper B) keeps a per-sample memory of the most recent gradient and forms a biased running average; SVRG (paper A) periodically refreshes a full-gradient snapshot and uses an unbiased control-variate update. The proof techniques differ substantially: SVRG analyses smoothness/control-variate algebra summed over an inner loop, while SAG constructs a quadratic Lyapunov function on an enlarged state vector.

matches.explanation: Both define the canonical finite-sum minimization problem $\min_w \frac{1}{n}\sum_i \psi_i(w)$ (SVRG) / $\min_x \frac{1}{n}\sum_i f_i(x)$ (SAG). Identical mathematical object; notation differs ($w$ vs $x$, $\psi_i$ vs $f_i$).

SVRG mentions least-squares and L2-regularized logistic regression as canonical instances of the finite-sum problem, while SAG promotes them to first-class problem nodes (regularized ERM, regularized logistic regression, regularized least squares). Same standard ML instances; SAG decomposes more finely because experiments and the line-search variant explicitly use the regularizer.

Both define $L$-smoothness (Lipschitz continuous gradient) of each component $\psi_i$ / $f_i$. SVRG uses the cocoercivity-style inequality form; SAG uses the Lipschitz-of-gradient form. These are equivalent for convex smooth functions and play identical roles. Confidence stays high despite SVRG's PDF-fallback caveat because the names and types align unambiguously.
Both define strong convexity of the objective $P$ / $g$ with constant $\gamma$ (SVRG) / $\mu$ (SAG). Standard definition; only the symbol for the constant differs.

Full-batch gradient descent baseline. SVRG cites it as Nesterov 2004; SAG also cites Cauchy/Nesterov and gives both the algorithm node (AP258.3) and the explicit iteration equation (EP258.1). Same external method; both are origin: external.

Vanilla SGD / Robbins-Monro baseline. Both papers list the iteration $w^{(t)} = w^{(t-1)} - \eta_t \nabla\psi_{i_t}(w^{(t-1)})$ and treat it as the stochastic baseline. SVRG's EP257.1 is the more general unbiased-estimator framework; both are the same SGD reference.

Central cross-paper match. SVRG cites SAG (Le Roux, Schmidt, Bach 2012) as an external prior variance-reduction method that achieves linear convergence by storing per-sample gradients; SAG (paper B) introduces it as its main contribution AP258.1 with the same algorithmic content. paper-origin (B) <-> external-origin (A) alignment, signal for the CF relationship: paper A frames SAG as the precedent its own SVRG simplifies.

The headline algorithms of the two papers. Both achieve linear convergence on smooth strongly-convex finite-sum problems by reusing past gradient information, but the construction is fundamentally different: SAG keeps an n-vector memory $y_i^k$ of the most recent component gradient and forms a biased running average $\frac{1}{n}\sum_i y_i^k$; SVRG keeps only one snapshot $\tilde w$ plus its full gradient $\tilde\mu$ and uses the unbiased control-variate update $\nabla\psi_{i_t}(w_{t-1}) - \nabla\psi_{i_t}(\tilde w) + \tilde\mu$. Same role in the theory, parallel complexity ($n\ln(1/\epsilon)$ examples), substantially different mechanism — this is the core CF pair.

Composite L2 step-block alignment justified by parent match (AP257.5 <-> AP258.1). Both decompose into Initialize -> Sample index -> Update -> Iterate, but the step contents differ in essential ways: SVRG has an outer/inner two-loop structure (refresh snapshot $\tilde\mu$ outside, run $m$ corrected SGD steps inside, then a snapshot-selection branch), whereas SAG has a single loop that updates the per-sample memory $y_i$ and the running sum each iteration. These differences are the substance of the competing-frameworks claim.

SVRG's Section 4 develops the SDCA connection: cites SDCA as a third variance-reduction method, restates the regularized problem in primal-dual form (ProbP257.2, EP257.4, EP257.5), and observes that SDCA is also a variance-reduction method whose update variance vanishes at the optimum (RP257.7). SAG (paper B) does not engage with SDCA or any dual perspective, so this entire SVRG sub-thread has no SAG counterpart.

The full-data snapshot gradient $\tilde\mu = \nabla P(\tilde w)$ computed once per outer stage is specific to SVRG's two-loop design. SAG never recomputes a full gradient: its $\frac{1}{n}\sum_i y_i^k$ is a memory-based stale running sum, not a snapshot. This is one of the defining differences between the two frameworks.

The two characteristic update equations. SVRG: $w^{(t)} = w^{(t-1)} - \eta(\nabla\psi_{i_t}(w^{(t-1)}) - \nabla\psi_{i_t}(\tilde w) + \tilde\mu)$, an unbiased control-variate of the full gradient. SAG: $x^{k+1} = x^k - \frac{\alpha_k}{n}\sum_i y_i^k$, a biased running average. Both are the iteration-defining equation of the parent algorithm; same role, mechanically different.

Unbiasedness of the SVRG update step is a characteristic property — and a notable distinction from SAG, whose update is biased (each $y_i^k$ is evaluated at a stale iterate). The corresponding SAG counterpart would be a remark that the update is biased; no such remark exists in paper B.

SVRG's auxiliary-function derivation $\tilde\psi_i(w) = \psi_i(w) - (\nabla\psi_i(\tilde w) - \tilde\mu)^\top w$ shows SVRG = vanilla SGD on a control-variate-shifted problem. This control-variate viewpoint is unique to the SVRG paper and has no analogue in SAG.

Both papers identify the variance-at-optimum mechanism but in different forms. SVRG's RP257.4 observes that the corrected gradient $\nabla\psi_{i_t}(w^{(t-1)}) - \nabla\psi_{i_t}(\tilde w) + \tilde\mu$ tends to $0$ as $\tilde w, w^{(t)} \to w^*$. SAG defines the variance at the optimum $\sigma^2 = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i \|f_i'(x^*)\|^2$ as a key constant in its convergence bound — this is precisely the residual variance that SAG accepts (it does not vanish) whereas SVRG drives it to zero by construction. The pair is analogous in role but the mechanisms differ; SAG also has a separate remark RP257.7 noting SDCA's vanishing variance, but RP258 has no direct counterpart.

Main convergence theorem. SVRG's TP257.1 gives geometric decay $\mathbb{E} P(\tilde w_s) - P(w^*) \leq \alpha^s [P(\tilde w_0) - P(w^*)]$ with explicit $\alpha$. SAG splits its result into two propositions (small step $\alpha = 1/(2nL)$ and large step $\alpha = 1/(2n\mu)$) giving $\mathbb{E}\|x^k-x^*\|^2 \leq (1-\mu/(8Ln))^k C_0$ and $\mathbb{E}[g(x^k)-g(x^*)] \leq C(1-1/(8n))^k$. All are linear-rate theorems on the same problem under the same assumptions, with rates that scale identically in $L,\mu,n$ at the leading order. Many-to-many because SAG's two parameter regimes both correspond to SVRG's single result.

Both proofs establish geometric contraction but use very different machinery, which is the heart of the CF classification. SVRG's PP257.1 bounds $\mathbb{E}\|v_t\|^2$ via smoothness and a control-variate identity, then sums across the inner loop and applies strong convexity. SAG's PP258.1 / PP258.2 build a quadratic Lyapunov function $Q(\theta^k)$ on the enlarged state $\theta^k = (y_1^k,\dots,y_n^k,x^k)^\top$, prove a one-step contraction $\mathbb{E} Q(\theta^k) \leq (1-\delta) Q(\theta^{k-1})$, then dominate the quantity of interest by $Q$ via Schur complement / convexity. Same target conclusion, fundamentally different proof technique.

Composite L2 step-block alignment justified by the parent proof matches above. The two step DAGs have only superficial parallels: both use Lipschitz/cocoercivity-type bounds early (PSP257.2 / PSP257.3 vs PSP258.3 via TP258.3) and both end with iterating a per-step contraction (PSP257.7 vs PSP258.6 / PSP258.13). But the intermediate steps are entirely different — SVRG's chain expands $\mathbb{E}\|w_t - w^*\|^2$ across an inner loop using $v_t$, while SAG's chain manipulates a Lyapunov $Q$ on an enlarged state via Lemma A.4 and Schur-complement domination. Listed as a single composite many-to-many entry per the v2 rule for L2 alignment.

Comparison of complexities/rates. SVRG's RP257.5 says SVRG processes $n\ln(1/\epsilon)$ examples to reach accuracy $\epsilon$, matching SAG and SDCA, vs $n^2\ln(1/\epsilon)$ for batch GD. SAG's ExP258.3 illustrates concrete contraction-factor numbers for FG, AFG, and SAG, and RP258.1 observes that SAG also recovers the SG $O(1/k)$ rate (with constant proportional to $n$). Same kind of observation — placing the new method on the rate landscape — but different specific comparisons.

Extensions to the smooth non-strongly-convex case ($O(1/T)$) and to nonconvex problems (local convergence, neural nets) are SVRG-specific contributions. SAG's analysis assumes strong convexity throughout and does not discuss either extension.

Empirical evaluation. Both papers compare their method against SGD/SG and a strong full-batch baseline on regularized logistic regression on a partly overlapping suite of datasets (rcv1, covtype/covertype). SVRG additionally compares against SDCA and includes a nonconvex neural-net experiment; SAG compares against AFG, L-BFGS, Pegasos, RDA, ESG, NOSG and runs a hand-tuned step-size second experiment. Per v2 rules examples receive a medium-confidence analogous match rather than per-dataset breakdowns.

SAG-specific definitions: the per-sample memory vector $y_i^k$, the enlarged Lyapunov state $\theta^k = (y_1^k,\dots,y_n^k,x^k)^\top$, and the selection function $S(j,i_{1:k})$. None has a counterpart in SVRG, which carries no per-sample state and uses no Lyapunov vector.

SAG bundles its standing assumptions (Lipschitz gradient, strong convexity, $y_i^0=0$ initialization) into a dedicated assumption node. SVRG states the same hypotheses inline within TP257.1's `assumptions` list rather than as a standalone node. The mathematical content is implicitly matched via DP257.1 <-> DP258.1 and DP257.2 <-> DP258.2; the standalone assumption-node is SAG-specific.

SAG with line search (SAG-LS), the L2 exact-regularizer recursion, and the line-search algorithm steps are practical SAG variants developed in Section 4 of paper B. SVRG does not propose an analogous line-search variant or exact-regularizer recursion.
Incremental Aggregated Gradient (IAG, Blatt et al. 2008) is a deterministic predecessor to SAG cited in paper B as the algorithm SAG randomizes. SVRG does not cite IAG.

Baseline algorithms cited only in SAG's experiments: AFG (Nesterov), Pegasos, RDA, ESG, NOSG, L-BFGS. All external-origin. SVRG's experimental section uses a different baseline set (SGD with various rate schedules, SDCA), so these have no counterpart on the A side.

SAG-specific lemmas. LP258.1 is the closed-form recursion for the quadratic Lyapunov $\theta$-form (the workhorse of both SAG proofs); LP258.2 is the SG-averaging bound used to initialize the large-step proof. Neither has a counterpart in SVRG, whose proof avoids the Lyapunov machinery and the SG warm-start.

External theorems cited by SAG: Nemirovsky-Yudin lower bound for stochastic strongly-convex optimization, Nesterov FG linear convergence, and Nesterov co-coercivity. SVRG does not lift these to node-level (SVRG's RP257.1 mentions analogous facts informally, but origin/role differ enough that no per-theorem match is warranted).

SAG-specific implementation/discussion remarks: the step-size $1/(16L)$ argument, the conjectured faster rate for $\alpha_k = 1/L$, and the memory-norm termination criterion. These are operationally specific to SAG's stored-gradient design and have no SVRG counterpart.

SVRG's RP257.1 is a textbook trade-off remark contrasting GD's linear rate with SGD's $O(1/t)$ sub-linear rate. SAG makes equivalent statements only inside the citations to TP258.1 / TP258.2 (treated as external theorems on the B side). Tagged as none rather than analogous because the matched B-side material is external-origin and a remark<->theorem cross-type match would be cosmetic.
